title: How Linux Remembers Its Kernel Stack Pointer (And Why You Should Care)
audience: Programmers curious about what happens inside a system call

slides.title: Whose stack?
slides.speaker_notes: Every system call enters the kernel with your stack pointer. The kernel refuses to use it. So where does its own stack come from?
slides.visual_beat: rsp register card pointing at the user stack; syscall arrow down into kernel mode; the user stack turns red; a dashed kernel stack with a question mark.

slides.title: The entry code
slides.speaker_notes: The entry code swaps G-S, stashes your stack pointer in a per-CPU slot, and loads the kernel's from another per-CPU variable: current top of stack.
slides.visual_beat: Real entry_SYSCALL_64 lines highlight in order; then the per-CPU area card: scratch slot receives user rsp, cpu_current_top_of_stack feeds rsp.

slides.title: Context switch
slides.speaker_notes: Every context switch rewrites that variable for the next thread, so it always points at the right kernel stack.
slides.visual_beat: Per-CPU slot points at thread A's kernel stack; the real __switch_to line appears; the pointer swings to thread B's stack.

slides.title: Why care
slides.speaker_notes: Why care? That stack is only sixteen kilobytes per thread. No deep recursion. No big local arrays. Overflow it, and a guard page catches it instead of silently corrupting memory.
slides.visual_beat: A 16 KiB stack bar fills with frames; frames overflow into a guard page that turns red and stops them.
